title: KV cache eviction / paging / prefix reuse deep dive - Nebula Labs
summary: Redwood SEs walked Nebula through KV cache internals and common eviction/paging causes. Discussed prefix reuse behaviors, long-context memory strategies, batching tradeoffs and quantization impact. Agreed to run a bench with Nebula's 50k token transcripts in a Dedicated pilot and share configs + security doc. Next steps: run benchmark, share recommended kernel/quantization profile, and schedule follow-up demo in two weeks.
transcript:
00:00 Maya Chen: alright hi everyone thanks for joining um this is Maya from Redwood, and with me is Devontae and Lena, we'll take you through our KV cache deep dive. can I confirm attendees?
00:08 Priya Rao: yep this is Priya, Marcus here, Sofia and Ethan as well. thanks for doing this.
00:14 Devontae Ruiz: great thanks Priya; quick agenda — we want to cover how KV cache is sharded, causes for eviction and paging, prefix reuse gotchas, then batching/quantization impacts and finally on-prem/VPC constraints. we'll leave time for your benchmarks. sound good?
00:26 Priya Rao: sounds perfect.
00:30 Devontae Ruiz: starting w high-level: our runtime keeps per-session KV caches keyed by sequence prefix; when you reuse prefixes across sessions we attempt to normalize, but differences in tokenization or special tokens can cause misses — so prefix reuse isn't always free.
00:47 Marcus Lee: can you explain how eviction is triggered? we've seen sudden latency spikes and evictions mid-conversation.
00:55 Devontae Ruiz: yeah there are a few triggers. primary is memory pressure on the GPU — when the total KV footprint for active sessions exceeds the budget we have an eviction policy. second is TTL-like behavior when a session is idle beyond retention. third is fragmenting of KV segments due to different sequence lengths causing inefficient packing, which can look like eviction.
01:16 Lena Ortiz: also important — batching strategy influences eviction. if you increase batch depth aggressively you'll hold more KV entries in memory longer which can push the pod into paging.
01:28 Priya Rao: we've been on a dedicated pool with 8xA100, and we saw evictions when ATL spikes; not sure if it's our prompt patterns or something else.
:01:38 Devontae Ruiz: makes sense; two quick checks: (1) are you using prefix anchors — e.g., stable system+user prompts — or highly variable prefixes? (2) what's your typical seq length distribution and tail — long tails cause bigger KV growth.
01:50 Priya Rao: we have a lot of multi-turn chats with variable user data appended, plus a few long-document summarization flows that go to 40k tokens.
01:59 Devontae Ruiz: 40k is a big one — our runtime supports long-context by paging KV to host memory and selectively reloading; paging reduces GPU memory pressure but adds latency for the pages pulled back. if paging thresholds are exceeded you'll see both eviction and latency spikes.
02:20 Marcus Lee: how do you page? is there an LRU?
02:24 Devontae Ruiz: yes, we maintain a hotset LRU for per-pod KV; when entries are paged to host we keep a compressed representation. rehydration is async for expected continuations, but abrupt random access patterns cause synchronous rehydrations and visible latency.
02:40 Sofia Alvarez: So prefix reuse — if two sessions share the same first 512 tokens, do you reuse the exact KV?
02:47 Lena Ortiz: we attempt to reuse where tokenization and model variant match. reuse is done at the shard level; identical token streams yield identical KV pointers and no recompute. but subtle token differences or function calls can diverge the cache. also when you have micro-prefix variations (e.g., timestamps or user IDs in the prompt) reuse effectiveness plummets.
03:10 Ethan Park: we noticed a pattern where evictions correlate with a spike in embedding requests from our ingestion pipeline — unrelated to the chat flow. could that interfere?
03:19 Devontae Ruiz: yes cross-workload interference is common on shared hosts. embeddings and generation sessions both consume KV/gpu memory; embeddings might pin memory for CPU->GPU transfers causing less room for KV. isolation (dedicated pools or resource pinning) helps.
03:33 Priya Rao: our Dedicated pool is logically isolated but still uses shared host pods for some helper services. what's the recommended isolation?
03:40 Devontae Ruiz: for production long-context workloads we recommend dedicated GPU hosts with pinned cache budgets per tenancy and enabling automatic prefix compaction. we'll share config snippets.
03:51 Marcus Lee: you mentioned prefix compaction — what is that?
03:54 Lena Ortiz: compaction merges near-identical prefixes to reduce redundant KV entries; it's heuristic-based — you'll get compaction savings when prompts differ only in non-semantic tokens. it can cause small correctness changes if the model relies on exact token offsets, so we let customers opt-in for aggressive compaction.
04:15 Priya Rao: ok that matches some anomalies we saw — a few responses were slightly off after compaction turned on in our PoC.
04:23 Devontae Ruiz: right we should pair compaction with golden prompt tests.
04:27 Maya Chen: quick note on quantization — per our experience 4-bit/8-bit quant can shrink model and KV overhead somewhat, but it also changes cache sizes and occasionally increases transient working set due to dequant/decompress stepping. it can help but bench is required.
04:42 Marcus Lee: interesting — we had thought quant always reduces memory.
04:45 Devontae Ruiz: usually it does for params, but KV caching interacts with kernel-level buffers. on certain kernels quantized matmuls allocate extra scratch space; that can temporarily increase peak usage.
04:58 Sofia Alvarez: is there guidance on batching size vs latency? our product wants sub-200ms p95 if possible.
05:04 Lena Ortiz: batching increases throughput but also increases KV retention time. With small latency SLOs you want shallow batching (batch size 1-4) and aggressive prefix caching; for throughput-focused offline jobs larger batches are fine. the runtime supports dynamic batching with latency-aware heuristics.
05:22 Ethan Park: do you give visibility into token-level latency and which requests triggered rehydration?
05:27 Devontae Ruiz: yes Console shows token-level timelines, rehydration events, and per-request cost. we'll show you a trace export after the call.
05:35 Priya Rao: we also saw prefix reuse failing when we switched tokenizer to byte-level for some regions. is that a tokenizer mismatch issue?
05:44 Devontae Ruiz: absolutely — tokenization must match the model runtime's tokenizer exactly. mismatches produce different token ids and thus different KV keys. ensure consistent preproc and inform us if you're applying custom token normalization so we can add safe prefix-mapping.
05:59 Marcus Lee: what's the typical eviction policy config we should look at?
06:03 Lena Ortiz: defaults: soft limit at 70% GPU KV budget triggers async paging; hard limit at 95% forces eviction of least-recent sessions. you can tune thresholds or set per-customer budgets on Dedicated.
06:20 Priya Rao: we've been seeing many 'forced evictions' logged. how do we debug whether it's fragmentation or real memory pressure?
06:28 Devontae Ruiz: check three signals: aggregate KV bytes per session distribution, number of small sessions causing fragmentation, and GPU memory headroom timeline. if headroom is consistently low and many medium-size sessions exist, fragmentation is likely. we can run a trace that simulates your workload and produce a fragmentation heatmap.
06:45 Marcus Lee: can caching be pinned for high-priority sessions? we have a revenue-critical chatflow.
06:50 Devontae Ruiz: yes on Dedicated we support pinned sessions with guaranteed KV reservation and pre-warming. that avoids eviction but reduces capacity for others.
06:59 Priya Rao: about paging — if pages go to host, are they encrypted at rest in an on-prem deployment?
07:05 Devontae Ruiz: good question — for Private deployments we integrate with your KMS and host encryption; host memory pages are kept in encrypted swap and access is logged. on VPC we also support HSM-backed KMS.
07:18 Maya Chen: quick pause, we'll share security docs.
07:20 Priya Rao: thanks.
07:23 Devontae Ruiz: back to performance: we recommend these immediate mitigations: reduce batch depth for latency SLO flows, enable prefix anchors (stable system/user tokens), opt into selective compaction after A/B testing, and apply per-session KV pinning for critical flows.
07:39 Marcus Lee: what's the cost impact of pinning?
07:42 Lena Ortiz: pinned sessions consume guaranteed memory so you trade capacity for predictability; cost is linear with the reserved GV per session times your reserved instances. we'll model with your traffic and send a cost delta after the bench.
07:54 Priya Rao: let's talk about bench plan — we want to reproduce the evictions and spikes.
07:59 Devontae Ruiz: recommended bench: 1) Replay representative seq length distribution (including your 40k docs) 2) Mix in embeddings and other background workloads to emulate interference 3) Run with both quantized and FP16 kernels, and with and without compaction 4) Capture token-level traces and memory timelines.
08:17 Marcus Lee: how long should the run be? we have daily ingestion bursts.
08:21 Devontae Ruiz: run steady-state for 30-60 minutes to capture fragmentation behavior, and a burst test for 5-10 minutes at peak QPS.
08:29 Ethan Park: we'll need the exact spec for the benchmark harness.
08:32 Lena Ortiz: we'll hand off a harness (workload.yml + replay driver) and a runbook; you'll run it in your Dedicated tenant or we'll run it from our lab with a sample dataset.
08:43 Priya Rao: can you also suggest kernel/quant settings?
08:46 Devontae Ruiz: yes our short recommendations: for 40k context use host-paging enabled, quant: try 4-bit with the newer int4 kernels (profiled) but run FP16 baseline; batching: dynamic with max latency 150ms for interactive flows; compaction: opt-in with 90% similarity threshold for initial tests. we'll include exact flags.
09:05 Priya Rao: any gotchas around function-calling and streaming? we rely heavily on streaming tokens to the client.
09:11 Devontae Ruiz: streaming holds open the session and the KV longer — that increases retention. function-calls can insert structured tokens which change tokenization boundaries — that can lead to reuse misses. consider using canonicalized function stubs in the prefix to improve reuse.
09:26 Marcus Lee: ok good. last bit: on-prem/VPC networking — do rehydration calls leave customer VPC?
09:32 Devontae Ruiz: for Private deployments nothing leaves the VPC. for Redwood-hosted Dedicated we route rehydration within the region and use encrypted tunnels; but for strict data residency you'd want Private.
09:44 Sofia Alvarez: thanks that's helpful.
09:46 Maya Chen: great recap: we'll (1) share the bench harness and runbook, (2) send initial config suggestions and security doc, (3) schedule a follow-up demo to review bench results in two weeks.
09:57 Priya Rao: sounds great — one ask: can you include the Console trace export template?
10:01 Devontae Ruiz: yes we'll attach the trace export and a sample heatmap.
10:06 Priya Rao: thanks everyone.
10:09 Maya Chen: thanks all, we'll follow up via the CRM with next steps.
10:14 [call ends]
next_steps: Maya to share benchmark harness + runbook (by 2026-05-14)
Devontae to provide kernel/quant config + flags (by 2026-05-14)
Redwood to run optional lab replay if Nebula shares sample dataset (coordinate via CRM)
Schedule follow-up demo to review bench results (target week of 2026-05-26)

Devontae Ruiz: prepare kernel and quantization recommendations and sample flags by 2026-05-14
